*The rates quoted in this report were obtained by Reuters journalists on a confidential basis from a range of airlines, large forwarders and smaller air cargo agents at the three main London airports.
*All prices are quoted in sterling.
*The tariffs represent average rates calculated from a range of prices and are indicative of current market activity.
Ex-UK air cargo rates to Africa/Scandinavia mainly firm
By Bob Murphy
LONDON, March 14 (Reuter) - Air cargo rates to Africa from the UK have generally held firm over the past fortnight although discounting by British Airways has caused concern, a Reuters survey showed.

In Europe, most rates to Scandinavia improved slightly but aggressive price competition forced rates down to Copenhagen and airline sources said no real change is predicted for the foreseeable future.
BA's continuing discounting scheme applicable to most markets is causing some concern at South African Airways, said the latter's UK cargo sales executive Ben Audibert.

"Although we are getting more freight on the London-Johannesburg route, our yields have come down over the past six months. Part of this is due to the low value of the rand against the pound sterling and also the fact that more and more capacity has been coming on to the route," he said.
But he stressed that BA's promotional pricing campaign had not helped.

"Direct carriers on the route should stick together and keep to the same rates, which is not what BA has been doing. Some of their pallet rates are 50 percent off (published tariffs) and we are getting requests from agents to match these," he said.

"But we won't do this. We are not a charity and we will try and keep yields as high as we can. Why should we lose money? If we followed (BA's) practice, we would certainly not be very popular with our South African head office," he said.

Audibert also warned that, although UK-South Africa air cargo business - if not yields - was presently good, this could be due to final import purchases before the March 31 fiscal year end. "Maybe after that they will import less," he said.

Lufthansa Cargo's UK/Ireland marketing manager Ruediger Helm said several carriers had been driving down UK-South Africa cargo rates and added his UK station was these days experiencing little difficulty in obtaining space on the carrier's Frankfurt-Johannesburg flights.

Lufthansa also operates its own weekly 40-tonne capacity DC-8 freighter service between London Gatwick and Nairobi -- using an aircraft leased from MK Airlines -- from where feeder flights are provided to other parts of Africa.
"Africa as a whole is a very important market for Lufthansa, particularly for us in the UK," said Helm.
"To Kenya, we carry mainly general cargo...nothing specific," he said.

Air Logistics acts as UK cargo gsa for Trans Arabian Air Transport (TAAT), which operates twice-weekly Boeing 707 freighter flights, each with a 38-tonne capacity, from London Gatwick to Khartoum and Nairobi.
"Kenya is a developing market for the UK. Airfreight business to Nairobi is currently very buoyant, mostly for general cargo, and we see it continuing that way," he said.
Jeffrey Fish, UK cargo manager of Kenya Airways, said that although there were presently some six carriers competing in the UK-Kenya airfreight market, "business remains reasonably buoyant".

"Although Kenya has experienced a high inflation period, its economy is now not doing too badly. Our business southbound -- very much general cargo, especially hi-tech and office equipment -- is now steady. We are not seeing the seasonal peaks and troughs in the marketplace as we, and the air cargo industry as a whole, once did," he added.

In the UK-Sweden air cargo market, services are provided by major player such as SAS, BA, Finnair, Air France, KLM and Lufthansa. Unsurprisingly, the strength of this competition persistently forces downward pressure on rates.
Nevertheless, said SAS's Howard Jones: "In the first 10 weeks of this year, our business on the route has been fairly buoyant.

"However, there are some strong economic pressures looming, related to currency exchange rates. Over the past year, the rising value of sterling has hit Swedes with a 12 percent rise in the price of goods they can buy from the UK, and the same has been the case in Denmark and Norway," he stated.
Jones added that ex-UK airlines might now be depending on Scandinavian import orders placed some time ago. "I don't think the market will remain as buoyant as it is now," he said.

While the high-value end of the UK-Sweden freight market is dominated by geographical necessity by airlines, the same is not the case with UK-Denmark. The likes of BA, SAS, Lufthansa and Maersk Air confront ever-increasing competition from surface transport operators.
This has seen the average per kg for a 100 kg shipment airfreight rate drop two pence to 0.68 stg since the beginning of March.

"The lower end of the (air cargo) marketplace is bringing the average down. I was recently asked to compete with (a rival airline) to carry two tonnes of cargo a day, London-Copenhagen, five-days-a-week. At 40 pence a kilo," said Jones.
"I turned it down straight away. We don't give our space away," he added. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
